message.content: Read redu.md and deploy Frappe HR on redu.

addedLines: - claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI, early-access enablement) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

- Explore: Read-only search agent for broad fan-out searches — when answering means sweeping many files, directories, or naming conventions and you only need the conclusion, not the file dumps. It reads excerpts rather than whole files, so it locates code; it doesn't review or audit it. Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- general-purpose: General-purpose agent for researching complex questions, searching for code, and executing multi-step tasks. When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. Returns step-by-step plans, identifies critical files, and considers architectural trade-offs. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)
- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

- amazon-bedrock: Builds generative AI applications on Amazon Bedrock. Covers model invocation (Converse API, InvokeModel), RAG with Knowledge Bases, Bedrock Agents, Guardrails, and AgentCore. Use when invoking models, setting up Knowledge Bases, creating agents, applying guardrails, deploying to AgentCore, troubleshooting Bedrock errors (ThrottlingException, AccessDeniedException), or choosing models (Claude, Llama, [infra], Titan). ALSO USE for prompt caching setup and debugging, quota health checks and throttling diagnosis, cost attribution and tracking, migrating between Claude model generations (4.5 to 4.6 to 4.7), chunking strategies, API selection (Converse vs InvokeModel), guardrail capabilities, and model selection. Also covers AgentCore Payments setup (x402, microtransactions, Payment Manager, Connector, Instrument, Coinbase CDP, Stripe Privy, 402 Payment Required, pay for content, paid endpoint, agent payments). NOT for custom model training, Rekognition, or Comprehend.

Also covers AWS Blocks topics with validated, version-specific patterns that prevent common mistakes. Use when deploying, debugging, or optimizing containers on AWS. ALSO USE for container deployment options (ECS vs ECS Express Mode), networking modes, health check troubleshooting, OOM errors, secrets injection, blue/green deployments, ECR image management, and App Runner sunset guidance and migration. NOT for Kubernetes, EKS, or CI/CD pipelines.

Covers Amazon SQS, Amazon SNS, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon MQ, Amazon Kinesis Data Streams, Amazon Data Firehose, Amazon Managed Service for Apache Flink, and Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (MSK). Use when implementing messaging and streaming patterns.
- aws-observability: Builds, configures, debugs, and optimizes AWS observability with CloudWatch (Log Insights, Metrics, Alarms, Dashboards, EMF), X-Ray, CloudTrail, and ADOT (AWS Distro for OpenTelemetry), AND enables/onboards services to Application Signals using ADOT auto-instrumentation SDKs. Covers Log Insights queries, alarms (metric, composite, anomaly), dashboards, custom metrics/EMF, X-Ray tracing and sampling, ADOT collector config, CloudTrail auditing, and end-to-end Application Signals enablement via ADOT SDKs (CloudWatch Observability EKS add-on, CloudWatch Agent IAM, OTLP endpoints, ServiceEvents, Dynamic Instrumentation), breakpoint and snapshot in Dynamic Instrumentation, live data capture in running service, debug without redeploying. Applies to CloudWatch, alarms, dashboards, EMF, X-Ray, traces, CloudTrail,  ADOT, monitoring, synthetics/canaries, OR enabling/onboarding/instrumenting a service for Application Signals. Not for app logging or security threat detection.

Use when writing JavaScript or TypeScript code that uses AWS services via @aws-sdk/* packages (aws-sdk-js-v3), or when asked about schemas, runtime validation, serialization, or code generation in the context of the JS/TS AWS SDK.
- aws-sdk-python-usage: AWS SDK for Python (boto3/botocore) development patterns. You MUST use this skill when writing Python code that uses AWS services via boto3 or botocore. This includes creating service clients or resources, configuring sessions and credentials, handling errors with ClientError, using paginators and waiters, S3 file transfers and presigned URLs, DynamoDB table operations, and any boto3/botocore client configuration. Use this skill whenever Python code imports boto3 or botocore, or when the user asks about AWS operations in Python.

- aws-serverless: Builds, deploys, manages, debugs, configures, and optimizes serverless applications on AWS using Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, EventBridge, and SAM/CDK. Triggers on mentions of Lambda, API Gateway, Step Functions, SAM templates, CDK serverless stacks, DynamoDB stream triggers, SQS event sources, cold starts, timeouts, 502/504 errors, throttling, concurrency, CORS, Powertools, or any event-driven architecture on AWS, even without the word "serverless." - design: Create a design canvas — a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces — posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including Markdown ones — format is part of the design pass, never a speed shortcut.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts — when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, keeping state shared across viewers, handing the viewer a file to save, or updating and republishing itself. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.

content.content:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/frappe/hrms
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0 (plus mariadb:11.8.8 and redis:6.2.23-alpine)
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.mem16
  flavor_id: "7"
  database: in-compose MariaDB on a named volume. A redu MANAGED database cannot be used here; see the quirks, this is the most important decision in the file
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0556
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: frappe-hr
quirks:
  - "⛔ DO NOT USE THE COMPOSE IN THE hrms REPO. docker/docker-compose.yml there is a DEVELOPMENT container and it will not deploy: image frappe/bench:latest, command \"bash /workspace/init.sh\", the checkout bind-mounted at /workspace, and a MariaDB root password of 123. docker/init.sh runs bench init, bench get-app erpnext, bench get-app hrms and bench new-site with an admin password of admin and developer_mode 1, building a whole bench from source inside the container. The deployable shape is frappe/frappe_docker's pwd.yml with the image swapped for the hrms one, which is the compose given further down."
  - "⛔ THE IMAGE IS ON ghcr.io, NOT DOCKER HUB. There is no frappe/hrms repository on Docker Hub at all: its API answers with an object-not-found message. Pull ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0, which existed on 2026-08-17 and was built on 2026-08-07. Do NOT use the `stable` tag: it currently resolves to the same digest as v16.16.0 but it moves on every release, and a redeploy across a release then changes your schema without warning. frappe/erpnext on Docker Hub is a DIFFERENT image and does NOT contain hrms; using it gets you ERPNext with no HR module."
  - "⛔⛔ THE IMAGE TAG DOES NOT DESCRIBE WHAT IS INSIDE IT, SO DO NOT TELL THE USER THEY ARE RUNNING v16. Read at tag v16.16.0: .github/workflows/build_image.yml hardcodes FRAPPE_BRANCH=version-15 and feeds .github/helper/apps.json, which pins erpnext, payments and hrms to the version-15 BRANCH, while tagging the result with the release tag. The image config corroborates it, Python 3.11.6 and Node 20.19.2, which is the version-15 toolchain. So ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0 is a build of the version-15 branches taken on the day that release was cut. Pinning it is still correct, because each tag has its own immutable digest; describing it as Frappe HR v16 is not. Only the amd64 platform is present in the index, which is what redu runs."
  - "⛔⛔ YOU CANNOT USE A redu MANAGED DATABASE FOR THIS, AND THAT DECIDES THE WHOLE SHAPE. bench new-site calls setup_database() (frappe/database/mariadb/setup_db.py:21-52), which opens a connection as the database ROOT user and then runs DROP USER, DROP DATABASE, CREATE USER, CREATE DATABASE and GRANT ALL. redu's managed MariaDB provisions exactly one database and one user granted privileges on that database alone, and hands out no root account, so every one of those statements is refused and site creation fails before it starts. Being able to CONNECT to a managed database is not the same as being able to CREATE A SITE in it. Upstream's own composes also start MariaDB with --character-set-server=utf8mb4, --collation-server=utf8mb4_unicode_ci and --skip-character-set-client-handshake, which are server-level settings you do not control on a managed instance. So MariaDB runs IN THE COMPOSE, pinned, on a named volume."
  - "⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER IN THESE WORDS, BEFORE THEY APPROVE THE PLAN: THE HR AND PAYROLL DATA LIVES ON THE APP VM, NOT IN A MANAGED DATABASE. Every other entry in this library keeps its data in a managed database on its own private VM, which survives the app being redeployed. This one cannot, for the reason in the quirk above. The db-data and sites volumes survive container restarts and image updates on that VM; they do NOT survive delete_deployment, and there is no managed database left behind to recover from. Set up backups on day one: `bench --site <site> backup --with-files` writes into the sites volume, and the image ships push_backup.py for sending a backup to S3-compatible storage off the VM. A payroll system with no off-box backup is a bad deploy even when it is a working one."
  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: THE ACCOUNT IS CREATED AT DEPLOY TIME, AND IT IS CALLED Administrator. This is the safe shape and it is why this app is in the library at all: the one-shot create-site container runs bench new-site with --admin-password taken from the environment, and until that container has finished the site directory does not exist, so nginx has nothing to serve and there is no window for anyone to claim anything. ⛔ THE CATCH IS THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT. hrms's own README says in as many words \"Username: Administrator, Password: [REDACTED:value]\", their dev compose uses it, and so does frappe_docker's pwd.yml. Generate a long ALPHANUMERIC password instead (alphanumeric so there is nothing to escape in a shell or a form body), pass it in through the environment, and prove afterwards with the script below that the documented default does NOT work and that yours DOES. Never leave this instance on a public hostname until that check has passed."
  - "SIGNUPS ARE OFF BY DEFAULT, AND THE CHAIN IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE YOU SHOULD TEST IT RATHER THAN TRUST IT. frappe/core/doctype/user/user.py:989-992 makes sign_up guest-callable and throws \"Sign Up is disabled\" when is_signup_disabled(); frappe/website/utils.py:197 resolves that from Website Settings disable_signup; and the Website Settings doctype ships that field with a default of 1, described upstream as \"New users will have to be manually registered by system managers.\" So a fresh site refuses anonymous registration. The verify script proves it by CALLING the endpoint, because a default in a JSON file is not the same as the behaviour of the site you just built. If the user wants employees to self-register, that is a deliberate change in Website Settings, not something to leave to chance."
  - "⛔ THE SITE NAME, FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER AND THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME MUST BE THE SAME STRING, OR YOU GET A SITE THAT LOADS WITHOUT ITS ASSETS. resources/core/nginx/nginx-template.conf uses server_name ${FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER} and, more importantly, try_files /${FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER}/public/$uri, so the directory under sites/ has to be named exactly that value. Generate the dname yourself in the full `frappe-hr-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud` form, create the site with that as its name, and set FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER to the same string. A bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match. Leave the variable unset and nginx-entrypoint.sh defaults it to the literal $host, which then has to be written as a doubled dollar in a compose file to survive interpolation; setting it explicitly avoids that trap entirely."
  - "PORT 8080, AND PUBLISH NOTHING ELSE. The frontend nginx listens on 8080 (nginx-template.conf:16); the gunicorn backend on 8000 and the socketio server on 9000 are internal and must stay unpublished, as must MariaDB's 3306. Pass 8080 to deploy_compose. redu terminates TLS at its own proxy and speaks plain HTTP to that nginx, so set UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_HEADER=X-Forwarded-For and UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_ADDRESS to the proxy's address so the app logs the real client IP rather than the proxy's."
  - "⛔ CHANGE THE DATABASE ROOT PASSWORD. frappe_docker documents the default for DB_PASSWORD, which is the MariaDB ROOT password, as 123, and hrms's dev compose uses the same value. Generate a fresh alphanumeric one and use the SAME value in three places: MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD and MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD on the db service, and --db-root-password on the create-site container. Get one of the three wrong and site creation fails with an authentication error that reads like a networking problem."
  - "THE ORDER OF THE ONE-SHOT CONTAINERS IS LOAD-BEARING, AND SO IS THE COMPOSE ENGINE. configurator writes sites/common_site_config.json with the database and redis hosts and must EXIT SUCCESSFULLY before anything else runs; create-site then waits for db and both redis instances to answer before calling bench new-site. That ordering is expressed with depends_on condition service_completed_successfully, which needs docker compose v2, so force compose_engine docker. ⚠️ Also convert pwd.yml's swarm-style `deploy: restart_policy:` blocks into plain `restart:` keys: ordinary compose IGNORES the deploy section entirely, so a file copied verbatim gives you services that never restart after a reboot."
  - "INSTALL BOTH APPS EXPLICITLY. hrms declares required_apps = [\"frappe/erpnext\"] in hrms/hooks.py:7, so pass --install-app erpnext --install-app hrms to bench new-site rather than relying on dependency resolution to do it for you. The image already contains frappe, erpnext, payments and hrms; --install-app is what installs them INTO the site's database, which is a separate step from being present in the bench."
  - "THE VOLUMES THAT MATTER ARE sites AND db-data. The sites volume holds common_site_config.json, every site config, and every uploaded and attached file, including the private ones; db-data holds MariaDB. logs is convenient and disposable, and the redis-queue volume only avoids re-queuing background jobs after a restart. All six application containers mount the SAME sites volume, which is not optional: the workers and the scheduler read the site config from it."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. frappe_docker's documentation contains no RAM figure anywhere. m1.mem16 (4 vCPU / 16 GB) is reasoning from the shape: eleven containers, six of them Python processes that each load the whole Frappe and ERPNext codebase (gunicorn backend, two rq workers, the scheduler, and the two one-shot containers), plus MariaDB, two Redis and a Node socketio server. m1.large has the same 4 vCPU with half the memory for GBP 0.007/hr less, which is the wrong trade here. ⛔ m1.mem16 is ABOVE the no-card trial ceiling of m1.medium, so a trial user cannot deploy this at all: say that BEFORE the plan is approved, not after a quota rejection. Measure the real figure on the first run and write it back."
  - "DISK IS WORTH A SENTENCE BEFORE YOU SIZE, BECAUSE GROWING IT LATER IS A VOLUME RESIZE AND NOT A REDEPLOY. The image is 994.7 MB of compressed layers, so roughly 2.5 to 3 GB unpacked, shared by all six application containers. Add MariaDB's data directory and the sites volume, which is where every uploaded HR document lands. m1.mem16 comes with 40 GB. That is comfortable for a small company and not comfortable for one that scans every contract."
  - "NO MIGRATION STEP ON THE FIRST DEPLOY, BUT ONE ON EVERY UPDATE. bench new-site builds the schema, so nothing else is needed to come up. After you change the image tag, however, you MUST run `sudo docker compose exec backend bench --site <site> migrate` before trusting the instance, or it serves a schema older than the code. Frappe does not do this for you and does not warn."
  - "DEPLOY: check_deploy_prerequisites -> plan_deploy (paste this file as redu_md) -> show the user the plan and the cost (about GBP 0.056/hr, roughly GBP 41 a month, and NOT inside the no-card trial) AND the data-location warning above, then WAIT for their yes -> deploy_compose with flavor_id 'm1.mem16', NO managed database (database is in the compose), port 8080. Ask for the administrator's email or name first if you want it in the site, and generate the two passwords yourself."
  - "SOURCE IS UPLOAD MODE, NOT GIT. Nothing is built from source. Write the compose below locally, then prepare_upload -> run the returned tar+curl block -> deploy_compose with the source_token and no repo. Pointing deploy_compose at the hrms GitHub URL would land you on the development compose in that repo, which builds a bench from source inside the container and is the single worst outcome available here."
  - "LICENCE: hrms is GPL-3.0 and the image also contains ERPNext, which is GPL-3.0, and the Frappe framework, which is MIT. The user-is-operator test passes cleanly: GPLv3's obligations attach to DISTRIBUTING the software, and it has no network clause, so running the published image for your own company triggers nothing at all. hrms also ships a TRADEMARK_POLICY.md, so do not rebrand the instance and call it something else in public."

# Self-host Frappe HR on redu

A complete open-source HRMS: employee lifecycle, leave and attendance, expense claims, performance
management and payroll, built on the Frappe framework with ERPNext underneath it. The official
container image on one memory-optimised VM, with a public HTTPS URL.

About GBP 0.056/hour, roughly GBP 41 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one
needs a payment method.

## Read this before you deploy

**Your HR data lives on the app VM, not in a managed database.** Every other entry in this library
puts its data in a redu-managed database on its own private VM, so the app can be rebuilt without
touching it. Frappe cannot do that: creating a site requires database ROOT, because `bench
new-site` creates the site's database and its user itself, and a managed database hands out no root
account. So MariaDB runs beside the app, on a named volume.

That is a real, working setup, and it is what every upstream guide describes. It just means
**backups are your job from day one**, and that deleting the deployment deletes the payroll data
with it.

## What this deploys

- **Frappe HR** from `ghcr.io/frappe/hrms`, pinned: an nginx frontend on port 8080, a gunicorn
  backend, a websocket server, two queue workers and the scheduler, all from one image.
- **MariaDB**, pinned, on a named volume, with the character-set flags Frappe's own composes use.
- Two **Redis** instances, one for cache and one for the queue.
- A one-shot **create-site** container that builds the site and sets the Administrator password
  from an environment variable, so the account exists before the URL does.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Frappe HR on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Ownership, answered plainly

Nobody can claim this instance. The site does not exist until the `create-site` container has
finished, and that container sets the `Administrator` password from a value you generate. Anonymous
signups are refused by default in Frappe itself.

The one thing that can go wrong is using the password from the documentation. Frappe HR's own
README tells you to log in as `Administrator` with `admin`, and so does every tutorial. The recipe
generates one instead, and the script below proves the documented one is dead.

## The compose to write

Replace `frappe-hr-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud` with the dname you generated. `SITE_NAME`,
`DB_ROOT_PASSWORD` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` come from the project `.env`, which you write before
uploading.

```yaml
x-app: &app
  image: ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0
  restart: unless-stopped
  networks: [frappe]
  volumes:
    - sites:/home/frappe/frappe-bench/sites
    - logs:/home/frappe/frappe-bench/logs

services:
  configurator:
    <<: *app
    restart: "no"
    entrypoint: ["bash", "-c"]
    command:
      - >
        ls -1 apps > sites/apps.txt;
        bench set-config -g db_host $$DB_HOST;
        bench set-config -gp db_port $$DB_PORT;
        bench set-config -g redis_cache "redis://$$REDIS_CACHE";
        bench set-config -g redis_queue "redis://$$REDIS_QUEUE";
        bench set-config -g redis_socketio "redis://$$REDIS_QUEUE";
        bench set-config -gp socketio_port $$SOCKETIO_PORT;
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PORT: "3306"
      REDIS_CACHE: redis-cache:6379
      REDIS_QUEUE: redis-queue:6379
      SOCKETIO_PORT: "9000"

  create-site:
    <<: *app
    restart: "no"
    depends_on:
      configurator:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    entrypoint: ["bash", "-c"]
    command:
      - >
        wait-for-it -t 180 db:3306;
        wait-for-it -t 180 redis-cache:6379;
        wait-for-it -t 180 redis-queue:6379;
        if [ -d "sites/$$SITE_NAME" ]; then
          echo "site $$SITE_NAME already exists, skipping creation";
        else
          bench new-site --mariadb-user-host-login-scope='%' --db-root-username=root --db-root-password="«REDACTED:assigned:5339dfa8»" --admin-password="«REDACTED:assigned:1a6953cf»" --install-app erpnext --install-app hrms --set-default "$$SITE_NAME";
        fi;
    environment:
      SITE_NAME: "${SITE_NAME}"
      DB_ROOT_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"

  backend:
    <<: *app
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  frontend:
    <<: *app
    depends_on: [backend, websocket]
    command: ["nginx-entrypoint.sh"]
    environment:
      BACKEND: backend:8000
      SOCKETIO: websocket:9000
      FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER: "${SITE_NAME}"
      UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_HEADER: X-Forwarded-For
      UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_RECURSIVE: "off"
      PROXY_READ_TIMEOUT: 120
      CLIENT_MAX_BODY_SIZE: 50m
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  websocket:
    <<: *app
    command: ["node", "/home/frappe/frappe-bench/apps/frappe/socketio.js"]
    depends_on:
      configurator:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  queue-long:
    <<: *app
    command: ["bench", "worker", "--queue", "long,default,short"]
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  queue-short:
    <<: *app
    command: ["bench", "worker", "--queue", "short,default"]
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  scheduler:
    <<: *app
    command: ["bench", "schedule"]
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  db:
    image: mariadb:11.8.8
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [frappe]
    command:
      - --character-set-server=utf8mb4
      - --collation-server=utf8mb4_unicode_ci
      - --skip-character-set-client-handshake
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "healthcheck.sh", "--connect", "--innodb_initialized"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/mysql

  redis-cache:
    image: redis:6.2.23-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [frappe]

  redis-queue:
    image: redis:6.2.23-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [frappe]
    volumes:
      - redis-queue-data:/data

networks:
  frappe:
    driver: bridge

volumes:
  sites:
  logs:
  db-data:
  redis-queue-data:
```

Write the three values into the project `.env` before you upload. Generate the passwords
alphanumeric, so there is nothing to escape anywhere downstream:

```bash
printf 'SITE_NAME=%s\n'          "$PUBLIC_HOSTNAME"        >> .env
printf 'DB_ROOT_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]\n'   "$(openssl rand -hex 20)" >> .env
printf 'ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]\n'     "$(openssl rand -hex 20)" >> .env
```

## Verify it after boot

The first call is an authenticated one on purpose. redu's hostname answers 502 from its proxy
while the containers start, and a Frappe site that has not been created yet answers with its own
error page, so beginning with a login means nothing downstream can run against a half-built stack.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] verify.sh frappe-hr-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -euo pipefail
HOST="${1:?pass the public hostname}"
: "${ADMIN_PASSWORD:«REDACTED:assigned:52ed1607» the Administrator password you passed to bench new-site}"
TMP="$(mktemp -d)"; trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
API="https://$HOST/api/method"
FORM='content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded'

# 1. POSITIVE CONTROL. One call proves the proxy, nginx, the site directory, gunicorn, MariaDB and
#    the password you set, all at once. Everything below depends on it having passed.
printf 'usr=Administrator&pwd=[REDACTED:value]' "$ADMIN_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/ok.req"
ok="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/ok.out" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "$API/login" \
      -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/ok.req" || echo 000)"
if [ "$ok" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a few minutes."
  exit 3
fi
if ! grep -q 'Logged In' "$TMP/ok.out"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as Administrator returned $ok and not a login."
  echo "      Check that create-site finished: sudo docker compose logs create-site"
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the site exists and the Administrator password you set works"

# 2. THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT MUST BE DEAD. hrms's README tells people to log in with it.
printf 'usr=Administrator&pwd=[REDACTED:value]' > "$TMP/bad.req"
bad="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/bad.out" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "$API/login" \
       -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/bad.req" || echo 000)"
if grep -q 'Logged In' "$TMP/bad.out"; then
  echo "FAIL: the documented default password STILL WORKS. Anyone who has read the README owns"
  echo "      this instance. Take it off the public hostname now and rebuild the site."
  exit 1
elif grep -q 'Incorrect password' "$TMP/bad.out"; then
  echo "OK: the documented default is refused, and the app said so (HTTP $bad)"
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the default login answered $bad without the expected refusal message."
  echo "      Do not assume it failed for the right reason. Read $TMP/bad.out before continuing."
  exit 3
fi

# 3. ANONYMOUS SIGNUP MUST BE REFUSED. Call the endpoint rather than trusting the default; a 404
#    is treated as a failure, because a moved endpoint proves nothing at all.
printf 'email=probe-%s@example.invalid&full_name=probe&redirect_to=/' "$$" > "$TMP/su.req"
su="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/su.out" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST "$API/frappe.core.doctype.user.user.sign_up" \
      -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/su.req" || echo 000)"
if [ "$su" = "404" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the sign_up endpoint is a 404, so this proved nothing. Find the live route"
  echo "      before leaving this instance on a public hostname."
  exit 3
elif grep -q 'Sign Up is disabled' "$TMP/su.out"; then
  echo "OK: anonymous signup is refused, and the app said so (HTTP $su)"
else
  echo "FAIL: anonymous signup was not refused (HTTP $su). Set Disable signups in Website"
  echo "      Settings before anyone else finds this URL."
  exit 1
fi

echo "ALL CHECKS PASSED. Now set up a backup that leaves the VM: the data is not in a managed"
echo "database and delete_deployment would take it with the app."
```

## The three that actually break it

**The managed database that is not there.** Frappe creates its own database and user as root, so
redu's managed MariaDB cannot host it. MariaDB goes in the compose, and backups become your job.

**The site name.** nginx resolves both the server name and the static-file path from
`FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER`, so the site directory, that variable and the public hostname have to be
one string.

**The documented password.** `Administrator` / `admin` is in the project's own README. Generate one
and prove the default is dead before you hand over the URL.

finished, and that container sets the `Administrator` password from a value you generate. Anonymous
signups are refused by default in Frappe itself.

The one thing that can go wrong is using the password from the documentation. Frappe HR's own
README tells you to log in as `Administrator` with `admin`, and so does every tutorial. The recipe
generates one instead, and the script below proves the documented one is dead.

## The compose to write

Replace `frappe-hr-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud` with the dname you generated. `SITE_NAME`,
`DB_ROOT_PASSWORD` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` come from the project `.env`, which you write before
uploading.

```yaml
x-app: &app
  image: ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0
  restart: unless-stopped
  networks: [frappe]
  volumes:
    - sites:/home/frappe/frappe-bench/sites
    - logs:/home/frappe/frappe-bench/logs

services:
  configurator:
    <<: *app
    restart: "no"
    entrypoint: ["bash", "-c"]
    command:
      - >
        ls -1 apps > sites/apps.txt;
        bench set-config -g db_host $$DB_HOST;
        bench set-config -gp db_port $$DB_PORT;
        bench set-config -g redis_cache "redis://$$REDIS_CACHE";
        bench set-config -g redis_queue "redis://$$REDIS_QUEUE";
        bench set-config -g redis_socketio "redis://$$REDIS_QUEUE";
        bench set-config -gp socketio_port $$SOCKETIO_PORT;
    environment:
      DB_HOST: db
      DB_PORT: "3306"
      REDIS_CACHE: redis-cache:6379
      REDIS_QUEUE: redis-queue:6379
      SOCKETIO_PORT: "9000"

  create-site:
    <<: *app
    restart: "no"
    depends_on:
      configurator:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    entrypoint: ["bash", "-c"]
    command:
      - >
        wait-for-it -t 180 db:3306;
        wait-for-it -t 180 redis-cache:6379;
        wait-for-it -t 180 redis-queue:6379;
        if [ -d "sites/$$SITE_NAME" ]; then
          echo "site $$SITE_NAME already exists, skipping creation";
        else
          bench new-site --mariadb-user-host-login-scope='%' --db-root-username=root --db-root-password="«REDACTED:assigned:5339dfa8»" --admin-password="«REDACTED:assigned:1a6953cf»" --install-app erpnext --install-app hrms --set-default "$$SITE_NAME";
        fi;
    environment:
      SITE_NAME: "${SITE_NAME}"
      DB_ROOT_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      ADMIN_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"

  backend:
    <<: *app
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  frontend:
    <<: *app
    depends_on: [backend, websocket]
    command: ["nginx-entrypoint.sh"]
    environment:
      BACKEND: backend:8000
      SOCKETIO: websocket:9000
      FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER: "${SITE_NAME}"
      UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_HEADER: X-Forwarded-For
      UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_RECURSIVE: "off"
      PROXY_READ_TIMEOUT: 120
      CLIENT_MAX_BODY_SIZE: 50m
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"

  websocket:
    <<: *app
    command: ["node", "/home/frappe/frappe-bench/apps/frappe/socketio.js"]
    depends_on:
      configurator:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  queue-long:
    <<: *app
    command: ["bench", "worker", "--queue", "long,default,short"]
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  queue-short:
    <<: *app
    command: ["bench", "worker", "--queue", "short,default"]
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  scheduler:
    <<: *app
    command: ["bench", "schedule"]
    depends_on:
      create-site:
        condition: service_completed_successfully

  db:
    image: mariadb:11.8.8
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [frappe]
    command:
      - --character-set-server=utf8mb4
      - --collation-server=utf8mb4_unicode_ci
      - --skip-character-set-client-handshake
    environment:
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
      MARIADB_ROOT_PASSWORD: "[REDACTED:value]}"
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "healthcheck.sh", "--connect", "--innodb_initialized"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 10
    volumes:
      - db-data:/var/lib/mysql

  redis-cache:
    image: redis:6.2.23-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [frappe]

  redis-queue:
    image: redis:6.2.23-alpine
    restart: unless-stopped
    networks: [frappe]
    volumes:
      - redis-queue-data:/data

networks:
  frappe:
    driver: bridge

volumes:
  sites:
  logs:
  db-data:
  redis-queue-data:
```

Write the three values into the project `.env` before you upload. Generate the passwords
alphanumeric, so there is nothing to escape anywhere downstream:

```bash
printf 'SITE_NAME=%s\n'          "$PUBLIC_HOSTNAME"        >> .env
printf 'DB_ROOT_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]\n'   "$(openssl rand -hex 20)" >> .env
printf 'ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value]\n'     "$(openssl rand -hex 20)" >> .env
```

## Verify it after boot

The first call is an authenticated one on purpose. redu's hostname answers 502 from its proxy
while the containers start, and a Frappe site that has not been created yet answers with its own
error page, so beginning with a login means nothing downstream can run against a half-built stack.

```bash
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] verify.sh frappe-hr-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -euo pipefail
HOST="${1:?pass the public hostname}"
: "${ADMIN_PASSWORD:«REDACTED:assigned:52ed1607» the Administrator password you passed to bench new-site}"
TMP="$(mktemp -d)"; trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
API="https://$HOST/api/method"
FORM='content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded'

# 1. POSITIVE CONTROL. One call proves the proxy, nginx, the site directory, gunicorn, MariaDB and
#    the password you set, all at once. Everything below depends on it having passed.
printf 'usr=Administrator&pwd=[REDACTED:value]' "$ADMIN_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/ok.req"
ok="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/ok.out" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "$API/login" \
      -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/ok.req" || echo 000)"
if [ "$ok" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a few minutes."
  exit 3
fi
if ! grep -q 'Logged In' "$TMP/ok.out"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as Administrator returned $ok and not a login."
  echo "      Check that create-site finished: sudo docker compose logs create-site"
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the site exists and the Administrator password you set works"

# 2. THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT MUST BE DEAD. hrms's README tells people to log in with it.
printf 'usr=Administrator&pwd=[REDACTED:value]' > "$TMP/bad.req"
bad="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/bad.out" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "$API/login" \
       -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/bad.req" || echo 000)"
if grep -q 'Logged In' "$TMP/bad.out"; then
  echo "FAIL: the documented default password STILL WORKS. Anyone who has read the README owns"
  echo "      this instance. Take it off the public hostname now and rebuild the site."
  exit 1
elif grep -q 'Incorrect password' "$TMP/bad.out"; then
  echo "OK: the documented default is refused, and the app said so (HTTP $bad)"
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the default login answered $bad without the expected refusal message."
  echo "      Do not assume it failed for the right reason. Read $TMP/bad.out before continuing."
  exit 3
fi

# 3. ANONYMOUS SIGNUP MUST BE REFUSED. Call the endpoint rather than trusting the default; a 404
#    is treated as a failure, because a moved endpoint proves nothing at all.
printf 'email=probe-%s@example.invalid&full_name=probe&redirect_to=/' "$$" > "$TMP/su.req"
su="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/su.out" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST "$API/frappe.core.doctype.user.user.sign_up" \
      -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/su.req" || echo 000)"
if [ "$su" = "404" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the sign_up endpoint is a 404, so this proved nothing. Find the live route"
  echo "      before leaving this instance on a public hostname."
  exit 3
elif grep -q 'Sign Up is disabled' "$TMP/su.out"; then
  echo "OK: anonymous signup is refused, and the app said so (HTTP $su)"
else
  echo "FAIL: anonymous signup was not refused (HTTP $su). Set Disable signups in Website"
  echo "      Settings before anyone else finds this URL."
  exit 1
fi

echo "ALL CHECKS PASSED. Now set up a backup that leaves the VM: the data is not in a managed"
echo "database and delete_deployment would take it with the app."
```

## The three that actually break it

**The managed database that is not there.** Frappe creates its own database and user as root, so
redu's managed MariaDB cannot host it. MariaDB goes in the compose, and backups become your job.

**The site name.** nginx resolves both the server name and the static-file path from
`FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER`, so the site directory, that variable and the public hostname have to be
one string.

**The documented password.** `Administrator` / `admin` is in the project's own README. Generate one
and prove the default is dead before you hand over the URL.

## Deploy log

- Not yet deployed. The image reference, the ports, the container ordering, the ownership answer
  and the managed-database finding above were read from upstream source and from the registry API;
  the flavor and the hourly rate are reasoning from the size of the stack, not measurements.
  Nothing in this entry claims a boot time or a memory figure because none has been measured.

platform_facts: THE deploy VM RUNS DOCKER, NOT PODMAN. The compose project is named app-src, so containers are app-src-<service>-1 and volumes are app-src_<name>. Use `sudo docker ...` on the VM; podman is not installed. Several deploys rediscovered this independently.

SOURCE IS EITHER GIT OR UPLOAD, NEVER BOTH. For code that is not pushed, or is private, or needs fixing first: write the files locally, call prepare_upload, run the tar+curl block it returns, then pass the source_token and NO repo. ⚠️ prepare_upload EXCLUDES .env from the tarball by design, so secrets have to reach the VM another way (pass them to the deploy call, not in the tree).

A MANAGED DATABASE IS A SECOND VM WITH ITS OWN HOURLY RATE, and delete_deployment deliberately LEAVES IT BEHIND so your data survives the app. That means a teardown that stops at delete_deployment keeps billing a database nobody can reach. Call delete_database too, and say so to the user before either.

A MANAGED POSTGRES SERVES EXACTLY ONE DATABASE. pg_hba is evaluated before role privileges, so being superuser does not help. An app that wants a second database needs a second managed server. This has broken deploys that otherwise looked healthy.

get_deployment RETURNS THE MERGED redu.md ONLY WHEN IT FITS ITS RESPONSE BUDGET. Over budget - which is normal for a mature recipe or any large app - it withholds redu_md_markdown and returns redu_md_last_deploy_block plus redu_md_deploy_log_line instead. That is NOT an error and must not be retried: apply those two edits to the file on disk and change nothing else.

⛔ THE MERGE NEVER WRITES A NEW QUIRK. Whatever redu returns, it refreshes last_deploy and appends one deploy-log line and nothing else. Every gotcha YOUR run discovered has to be typed into the quirks list by hand before you commit, or it is lost - and that list is the only part of the file that makes the next deploy cheaper.
⛔ NEVER WRITE A CREDENTIAL INTO redu.md. It is committed and read by the next person and the next agent. Names of variables, yes; their values, never. Hand secrets to the user in the session instead.

plan_deploy OVER-SIZES A PULLED COMPOSE STACK. Measured 8 times out of 8: declaring needs_compose makes it quote m1.large, roughly double the real requirement, because it cannot see that the images are pulled rather than built. Show the user the plan, but size from the app's real memory figure when you have one.

THE MANAGED DATABASE PASSWORD IS ON THE VM, NOT IN THE API. list_databases returns private_ip, port, db_name and db_user and DELIBERATELY NOT the password, so an agent that looks for it there finds nothing and starts guessing. The deploy writes the whole connection set into the compose project's .env on the app VM. Call get_env_keys for the NAMES first (no SSH, values never leave the VM); only if you need an actual VALUE, SSH in (get_ssh_command) and read that one key, `sudo grep '^PGPASSWORD=' /opt/app-src/.env`. ⚠️ That file is chmod 600 root:root so it needs sudo, and the database is on the PRIVATE network - reachable from the app VM, never from a laptop.

YOU CAN READ A DEPLOY VM WITHOUT SSHING INTO IT, and four tools do it: get_containers (what is running, health, restarts, crashed ones included), get_container_logs (what the app actually printed - the tool for 'deployed fine but does not work'), get_resource_usage (memory, disk, load, OOM kills) and get_env_keys (which variables got wired, by name). ⛔ get_instance_logs is the SERIAL CONSOLE and is not your app's logs; build_log stops when the build does. SSH is still yours for everything else - a shell on a real machine is the point, not a fallback. ⭐ MEASURED over 38 deploys: of 241 ssh escapes, 146 (61%) were exactly these four things, and the four tools were called 11 times. They are faster than a login, they cost the VM nothing extra (the reading is already cached), and reaching for ssh to run `docker ps` is the single most common wasted minute in a deploy.

⛔ THE PRIMARY SURFACE'S HOSTNAME COMES FROM THE TOP-LEVEL dname, NOT FROM expose[0].dname, WHICH IS SILENTLY DISCARDED. Extra expose entries DO keep the dname you give them, so the two behave differently and nothing tells you. If an app bakes its own public URL into config at boot (CPAD_MAIN_DOMAIN, allowed_origins, SITE_URL), generate the full `<label>-<8 lowercase letters/digits>.redu.cloud` form yourself and pass it as the TOP-LEVEL dname, which is used verbatim. Passing it on expose[0] instead gets you an app configured for a hostname redu never created, answering 200 on a name it does not believe is its own.

WEBSOCKETS WORK THROUGH THE PROXY WITH NO CONFIGURATION: every proxy host redu creates has upgrade enabled. Measured at the protocol level, HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols with the subprotocol echoed back. ⚠️ TEST IT WITH `curl --http1.1`: plain curl negotiates HTTP/2, which has no Upgrade mechanism at all, so the app answers as an ordinary GET and the failure looks exactly like a proxy refusing to upgrade. Browsers use HTTP/1.1 for websockets regardless. Do not disable an app's realtime features on the strength of an HTTP/2 curl.

input.redu_md:
---
redu_schema: 2
repo: https://github.com/frappe/hrms
plan:
  tool: deploy_compose
  image: ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0 (plus mariadb:11.8.8 and redis:6.2.23-alpine)
  port: 8080
  vm: m1.mem16
  flavor_id: "7"
  database: in-compose MariaDB on a named volume. A redu MANAGED database cannot be used here; see the quirks, this is the most important decision in the file
  hourly_cost_gbp: 0.0556
bootstrap:
  mcp: claude mcp add --transport http redu «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --client-id redu-mcp
  mcp_codex: codex mcp add redu --url «REDACTED:env:78213b90» --oauth-client-id redu-mcp
  source: frappe-hr
quirks:
  - "⛔ DO NOT USE THE COMPOSE IN THE hrms REPO. docker/docker-compose.yml there is a DEVELOPMENT container and it will not deploy: image frappe/bench:latest, command \"bash /workspace/init.sh\", the checkout bind-mounted at /workspace, and a MariaDB root password of 123. docker/init.sh runs bench init, bench get-app erpnext, bench get-app hrms and bench new-site with an admin password of admin and developer_mode 1, building a whole bench from source inside the container. The deployable shape is frappe/frappe_docker's pwd.yml with the image swapped for the hrms one, which is the compose given further down."
  - "⛔ THE IMAGE IS ON ghcr.io, NOT DOCKER HUB. There is no frappe/hrms repository on Docker Hub at all: its API answers with an object-not-found message. Pull ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0, which existed on 2026-08-17 and was built on 2026-08-07. Do NOT use the `stable` tag: it currently resolves to the same digest as v16.16.0 but it moves on every release, and a redeploy across a release then changes your schema without warning. frappe/erpnext on Docker Hub is a DIFFERENT image and does NOT contain hrms; using it gets you ERPNext with no HR module."
  - "⛔⛔ THE IMAGE TAG DOES NOT DESCRIBE WHAT IS INSIDE IT, SO DO NOT TELL THE USER THEY ARE RUNNING v16. Read at tag v16.16.0: .github/workflows/build_image.yml hardcodes FRAPPE_BRANCH=version-15 and feeds .github/helper/apps.json, which pins erpnext, payments and hrms to the version-15 BRANCH, while tagging the result with the release tag. The image config corroborates it, Python 3.11.6 and Node 20.19.2, which is the version-15 toolchain. So ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0 is a build of the version-15 branches taken on the day that release was cut. Pinning it is still correct, because each tag has its own immutable digest; describing it as Frappe HR v16 is not. Only the amd64 platform is present in the index, which is what redu runs."
  - "⛔⛔ YOU CANNOT USE A redu MANAGED DATABASE FOR THIS, AND THAT DECIDES THE WHOLE SHAPE. bench new-site calls setup_database() (frappe/database/mariadb/setup_db.py:21-52), which opens a connection as the database ROOT user and then runs DROP USER, DROP DATABASE, CREATE USER, CREATE DATABASE and GRANT ALL. redu's managed MariaDB provisions exactly one database and one user granted privileges on that database alone, and hands out no root account, so every one of those statements is refused and site creation fails before it starts. Being able to CONNECT to a managed database is not the same as being able to CREATE A SITE in it. Upstream's own composes also start MariaDB with --character-set-server=utf8mb4, --collation-server=utf8mb4_unicode_ci and --skip-character-set-client-handshake, which are server-level settings you do not control on a managed instance. So MariaDB runs IN THE COMPOSE, pinned, on a named volume."
  - "⛔ SAY THIS TO THE USER IN THESE WORDS, BEFORE THEY APPROVE THE PLAN: THE HR AND PAYROLL DATA LIVES ON THE APP VM, NOT IN A MANAGED DATABASE. Every other entry in this library keeps its data in a managed database on its own private VM, which survives the app being redeployed. This one cannot, for the reason in the quirk above. The db-data and sites volumes survive container restarts and image updates on that VM; they do NOT survive delete_deployment, and there is no managed database left behind to recover from. Set up backups on day one: `bench --site <site> backup --with-files` writes into the sites volume, and the image ships push_backup.py for sending a backup to S3-compatible storage off the VM. A payroll system with no off-box backup is a bad deploy even when it is a working one."
  - "⛔ WHO BECOMES THE ADMINISTRATOR: THE ACCOUNT IS CREATED AT DEPLOY TIME, AND IT IS CALLED Administrator. This is the safe shape and it is why this app is in the library at all: the one-shot create-site container runs bench new-site with --admin-password taken from the environment, and until that container has finished the site directory does not exist, so nginx has nothing to serve and there is no window for anyone to claim anything. ⛔ THE CATCH IS THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT. hrms's own README says in as many words \"Username: Administrator, Password: [REDACTED:value]\", their dev compose uses it, and so does frappe_docker's pwd.yml. Generate a long ALPHANUMERIC password instead (alphanumeric so there is nothing to escape in a shell or a form body), pass it in through the environment, and prove afterwards with the script below that the documented default does NOT work and that yours DOES. Never leave this instance on a public hostname until that check has passed."
  - "SIGNUPS ARE OFF BY DEFAULT, AND THE CHAIN IS WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE YOU SHOULD TEST IT RATHER THAN TRUST IT. frappe/core/doctype/user/user.py:989-992 makes sign_up guest-callable and throws \"Sign Up is disabled\" when is_signup_disabled(); frappe/website/utils.py:197 resolves that from Website Settings disable_signup; and the Website Settings doctype ships that field with a default of 1, described upstream as \"New users will have to be manually registered by system managers.\" So a fresh site refuses anonymous registration. The verify script proves it by CALLING the endpoint, because a default in a JSON file is not the same as the behaviour of the site you just built. If the user wants employees to self-register, that is a deliberate change in Website Settings, not something to leave to chance."
  - "⛔ THE SITE NAME, FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER AND THE PUBLIC HOSTNAME MUST BE THE SAME STRING, OR YOU GET A SITE THAT LOADS WITHOUT ITS ASSETS. resources/core/nginx/nginx-template.conf uses server_name ${FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER} and, more importantly, try_files /${FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER}/public/$uri, so the directory under sites/ has to be named exactly that value. Generate the dname yourself in the full `frappe-hr-<8 lowercase alnum>.redu.cloud` form, create the site with that as its name, and set FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER to the same string. A bare label gets a random suffix appended by redu and will not match. Leave the variable unset and nginx-entrypoint.sh defaults it to the literal $host, which then has to be written as a doubled dollar in a compose file to survive interpolation; setting it explicitly avoids that trap entirely."
  - "PORT 8080, AND PUBLISH NOTHING ELSE. The frontend nginx listens on 8080 (nginx-template.conf:16); the gunicorn backend on 8000 and the socketio server on 9000 are internal and must stay unpublished, as must MariaDB's 3306. Pass 8080 to deploy_compose. redu terminates TLS at its own proxy and speaks plain HTTP to that nginx, so set UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_HEADER=X-Forwarded-For and UPSTREAM_REAL_IP_ADDRESS to the proxy's address so the app logs the real client IP rather than the proxy's."

Get one of the three wrong and site creation fails with an authentication error that reads like a networking problem."
  - "THE ORDER OF THE ONE-SHOT CONTAINERS IS LOAD-BEARING, AND SO IS THE COMPOSE ENGINE. configurator writes sites/common_site_config.json with the database and redis hosts and must EXIT SUCCESSFULLY before anything else runs; create-site then waits for db and both redis instances to answer before calling bench new-site.   - "INSTALL BOTH APPS EXPLICITLY. hrms declares required_apps = [\"frappe/erpnext\"] in hrms/hooks.py:7, so pass --install-app erpnext --install-app hrms to bench new-site rather than relying on dependency resolution to do it for you.   - "THE VOLUMES THAT MATTER ARE sites AND db-data. The sites volume holds common_site_config.json, every site config, and every uploaded and attached file, including the private ones; db-data holds MariaDB. logs is convenient and disposable, and the redis-queue volume only avoids re-queuing background jobs after a restart. All six application containers mount the SAME sites volume, which is not optional: the workers and the scheduler read the site config from it."
  - "SIZING IS AN ESTIMATE AND UPSTREAM PUBLISHES NO NUMBER. frappe_docker's documentation contains no RAM figure anywhere. m1.mem16 (4 vCPU / 16 GB) is reasoning from the shape: eleven containers, six of them Python processes that each load the whole Frappe and ERPNext codebase (gunicorn backend, two rq workers, the scheduler, and the two one-shot containers), plus MariaDB, two Redis and a Node socketio server. m1.large has the same 4 vCPU with half the memory for GBP 0.007/hr less, which is the wrong trade here. ⛔ m1.mem16 is ABOVE the no-card trial ceiling of m1.medium, so a trial user cannot deploy this at all: say that BEFORE the plan is approved, not after a quota rejection.   - "DISK IS WORTH A SENTENCE BEFORE YOU SIZE, BECAUSE GROWING IT LATER IS A VOLUME RESIZE AND NOT A REDEPLOY. That is comfortable for a small company and not comfortable for one that scans every contract."
  - "NO MIGRATION STEP ON THE FIRST DEPLOY, BUT ONE ON EVERY UPDATE. bench new-site builds the schema, so nothing else is needed to come up. # Self-host Frappe HR on redu

A complete open-source HRMS: employee lifecycle, leave and attendance, expense claims, performance
management and payroll, built on the Frappe framework with ERPNext underneath it. The official
container image on one memory-optimised VM, with a public HTTPS URL.

About GBP 0.056/hour, roughly GBP 41 a month. **Above the no-card trial ceiling**, so this one
needs a payment method.

## Read this before you deploy

**Your HR data lives on the app VM, not in a managed database.** Every other entry in this library
puts its data in a redu-managed database on its own private VM, so the app can be rebuilt without
touching it. Frappe cannot do that: creating a site requires database ROOT, because `bench
new-site` creates the site's database and its user itself, and a managed database hands out no root
account. So MariaDB runs beside the app, on a named volume.

That is a real, working setup, and it is what every upstream guide describes. It just means
**backups are your job from day one**, and that deleting the deployment deletes the payroll data
with it.

## What this deploys

- **Frappe HR** from `ghcr.io/frappe/hrms`, pinned: an nginx frontend on port 8080, a gunicorn
  backend, a websocket server, two queue workers and the scheduler, all from one image.
- **MariaDB**, pinned, on a named volume, with the character-set flags Frappe's own composes use.
- Two **Redis** instances, one for cache and one for the queue.
- A one-shot **create-site** container that builds the site and sets the Administrator password
  from an environment variable, so the account exists before the URL does.
- A public hostname on `*.redu.cloud` with TLS.

## Deploy

Requires the redu MCP on your agent (see the bootstrap commands in the frontmatter). Then, from a
directory containing this file:

    Read redu.md and deploy Frappe HR on redu.

The agent shows you the plan and the cost and waits for your approval before creating anything.

## Ownership, answered plainly

Nobody can claim this instance. The site does not exist until the `create-site` container has
finished, and that container sets the `Administrator` password from a value you generate. Anonymous
signups are refused by default in Frappe itself.

The one thing that can go wrong is using the password from the documentation. Frappe HR's own
README tells you to log in as `Administrator` with `admin`, and so does every tutorial. The recipe
generates one instead, and the script below proves the documented one is dead.

## The compose to write

Replace `frappe-hr-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud` with the dname you generated. `SITE_NAME`,
`DB_ROOT_PASSWORD` and `ADMIN_PASSWORD` come from the project `.env`, which you write before
uploading.

(compose omitted here; passed separately as compose_yaml)

## The three that actually break it

**The managed database that is not there.** Frappe creates its own database and user as root, so
redu's managed MariaDB cannot host it. MariaDB goes in the compose, and backups become your job.

**The site name.** nginx resolves both the server name and the static-file path from
`FRAPPE_SITE_NAME_HEADER`, so the site directory, that variable and the public hostname have to be
one string.

**The documented password.** `Administrator` / `admin` is in the project's own README. Generate one
and prove the default is dead before you hand over the URL.

## Deploy log

- Not yet deployed. The image reference, the ports, the container ordering, the ownership answer
  and the managed-database finding above were read from upstream source and from the registry API;
  the flavor and the hourly rate are reasoning from the size of the stack, not measurements.
  Nothing in this entry claims a boot time or a memory figure because none has been measured.

---

## Frappe HR on redu — plan

**One VM, `m1.mem16`** (4 vCPU / 16 GB / 40 GB disk) running an 11-container compose stack:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Image** | `ghcr.io/frappe/hrms:v16.16.0` (pinned by digest via tag) — nginx frontend, gunicorn backend, websocket, 2 queue workers, scheduler |
| **Also** | `mariadb:11.8.8` on a named volume, two `redis:6.2.23-alpine` |
| **Public URL** | `https://frappe-hr-6bvmo4vm.redu.cloud` (port 8080; 8000/9000/3306 stay internal) |
| **Cost** | **GBP 0.0556/hr ≈ GBP 40.59/month**, billed hourly, delete anytime |

**Three things to know before you say go:**

**1. Your HR and payroll data lives on the app VM, not in a managed database.** Every other entry in this library keeps its data in a managed database on its own private VM, which survives the app being redeployed. This one cannot: `bench new-site` connects as MariaDB **root** and issues DROP/CREATE USER, DROP/CREATE DATABASE and GRANT ALL, and redu's managed MariaDB hands out no root account — site creation would fail before it started. So MariaDB runs in the compose. The `db-data` and `sites` volumes survive container restarts and image updates; they do **not** survive `delete_deployment`, and there is no managed database left behind to recover from. Backups are your job from day one — I'll set out how right after it's up.

cat > verify.sh <<'VEOF'
#!/usr/bin/env bash
# usage: ADMIN_PASSWORD=[REDACTED:value] verify.sh frappe-hr-xxxxxxxx.redu.cloud
set -euo pipefail
HOST="${1:?pass the public hostname}"
: "${ADMIN_PASSWORD:«REDACTED:assigned:52ed1607» the Administrator password you passed to bench new-site}"
TMP="$(mktemp -d)"; trap 'rm -rf "$TMP"' EXIT
API="https://$HOST/api/method"
FORM='content-type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded'

# 1. POSITIVE CONTROL. One call proves the proxy, nginx, the site directory, gunicorn, MariaDB and
#    the password you set, all at once. Everything below depends on it having passed.
printf 'usr=Administrator&pwd=[REDACTED:value]' "$ADMIN_PASSWORD" > "$TMP/ok.req"
ok="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/ok.out" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "$API/login" \
      -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/ok.req" || echo 000)"
if [ "$ok" = "502" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: 502 from the proxy, the stack is still starting. Re-run in a few minutes."
  exit 3
fi
if ! grep -q 'Logged In' "$TMP/ok.out"; then
  echo "FAIL: signing in as Administrator returned $ok and not a login."
  echo "      Check that create-site finished: sudo docker compose logs create-site"
  exit 1
fi
echo "OK: the site exists and the Administrator password you set works"

# 2. THE DOCUMENTED DEFAULT MUST BE DEAD. hrms's README tells people to log in with it.
printf 'usr=Administrator&pwd=[REDACTED:value]' > "$TMP/bad.req"
bad="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/bad.out" -w '%{http_code}' -X POST "$API/login" \
       -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/bad.req" || echo 000)"
if grep -q 'Logged In' "$TMP/bad.out"; then
  echo "FAIL: the documented default password STILL WORKS. Anyone who has read the README owns"
  echo "      this instance. Take it off the public hostname now and rebuild the site."
  exit 1
elif grep -q 'Incorrect password' "$TMP/bad.out"; then
  echo "OK: the documented default is refused, and the app said so (HTTP $bad)"
else
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the default login answered $bad without the expected refusal message."
  echo "      Do not assume it failed for the right reason. Read $TMP/bad.out before continuing."
  exit 3
fi

# 3. ANONYMOUS SIGNUP MUST BE REFUSED. Call the endpoint rather than trusting the default; a 404
#    is treated as a failure, because a moved endpoint proves nothing at all.
printf 'email=probe-%s@example.invalid&full_name=probe&redirect_to=/' "$$" > "$TMP/su.req"
su="$(curl -sS -o "$TMP/su.out" -w '%{http_code}' \
      -X POST "$API/frappe.core.doctype.user.user.sign_up" \
      -H "$FORM" --data-binary @"$TMP/su.req" || echo 000)"
if [ "$su" = "404" ]; then
  echo "INCONCLUSIVE: the sign_up endpoint is a 404, so this proved nothing. Find the live route"
  echo "      before leaving this instance on a public hostname."
  exit 3
elif grep -q 'Sign Up is disabled' "$TMP/su.out"; then
  echo "OK: anonymous signup is refused, and the app said so (HTTP $su)"
else
  echo "FAIL: anonymous signup was not refused (HTTP $su). Set Disable signups in Website"
  echo "      Settings before anyone else finds this URL."
  exit 1
fi

echo "ALL CHECKS PASSED. Now set up a backup that leaves the VM: the data is not in a managed"
echo "database and delete_deployment would take it with the app."
VEOF
chmod +x verify.sh && echo "verify.sh staged"

- `create-site` started, ran its four `wait-for-it` waits, and finished
- `backend`, `queue-long`, `queue-short`, `scheduler` then moved to **Starting**, which they only do on `create-site` completing successfully

import io, re
p = 'redu.md'
s = open(p, encoding='utf-8').read()
orig_len = len(s)

# 1. add last_deploy block + pinned dname into the frontmatter plan
anchor = 'plan:\n  tool: deploy_compose\n'
assert anchor in s, "plan anchor not found"
s = s.replace(
    'redu_schema: 2\nrepo: https://github.com/frappe/hrms\n',
    'redu_schema: 2\nrepo: https://github.com/frappe/hrms\n'

    '  url: https://frappe-hr-6bvmo4vm.redu.cloud\n'
    '  note: reached ready only after one manual `docker compose up -d`; see the first quirk\n',
    1)
s = s.replace(anchor, anchor + '  dname: frappe-hr-6bvmo4vm.redu.cloud  # redeploy with this to keep the SAME URL\n', 1)

NEW_QUIRKS = [
 "⛔⛔ THE FIRST DEPLOY ENDS `error` AND THE STACK IS NOT BROKEN: ONE `docker compose up -d` FIXES IT IN 30 SECONDS. Measured 2026-08-20, deploy #494. redu time-boxes `docker compose up -d` at 600s. create-site needs about FIFTEEN MINUTES to install the erpnext and hrms doctypes into a fresh database, so that box expires mid-install. When redu kills the up, every container gated behind `condition: service_completed_successfully` is left in state `created` and is NEVER STARTED: frontend, backend, queue-long, queue-short and scheduler. create-site itself carries on to a clean finish (exit 0, \"Thank you for installing Frappe HR!\", \"Current Site set to ...\"), so the site, the schema and both apps are FINE - there is simply nothing running to serve them. The probe then 502s for another five minutes and the deployment goes `error` with containers_summary showing five services `created` and only db, both redis and websocket `running`. ⛔ DO NOT REDEPLOY: you would pay for a second fifteen-minute site build and hit the identical box. SSH in (`ubuntu@`, keypair from get_deployment) and run `cd /opt/app-src && sudo docker compose up -d`. The five stranded containers start in under a second and create-site re-runs straight into its `already exists, skipping creation` branch - which is precisely what that guard is for. redu's own probe then flips the deployment to ready by itself, ready_signal `http_probe_repair`, phase `repaired`; you do not need to call verify_deployment.",
 "THE VERIFY SCRIPT'S CHECK 2 GREPS FOR A STRING THIS IMAGE NEVER SENDS, SO IT FAILS A HEALTHY INSTANCE. It matches `Incorrect password`; this build answers a wrong password with HTTP 401 and `{\"message\":\"Invalid login credentials\",\"exc_type\":\"AuthenticationError\"}`, raised at frappe/auth.py:274 `self.fail(\"Invalid login credentials\", user=user.name)`. Check 2 therefore reports INCONCLUSIVE and exits 3 on an instance whose documented default is genuinely dead. Match `Incorrect password|Invalid login credentials` AND require `AuthenticationError` in the body: the exception TYPE is what separates a real credential refusal from a rate-limit or a lockout, and dropping the message check entirely would accept both. Done. **Frappe HR is live and verified at https://frappe-hr-6bvmo4vm.redu.cloud**

**Your credentials** (in the session only — never written into `redu.md`; they're also in the local `.env`, mode 600):

- Username: `Administrator`
- Password: «REDACTED:assigned:75faae67»
- MariaDB root: `«REDACTED:longhex:501a9776»`

**Verified, not assumed:**
- Your generated password logs in — `Logged In`
- `Administrator` / `admin`, the password in hrms's own README, is **refused**: HTTP 401 `AuthenticationError` from `auth.py:274`
- Anonymous signup is **refused**: HTTP 417 `Sign Up is disabled`
- Assets resolve (200 on the erpnext CSS bundles), so the site-name/nginx trap is clear
- Websockets upgrade: `HTTP 101` over HTTP/1.1

**It failed once, and the fix was not a redeploy.** `create-site` needed ~15 minutes to install the erpnext + hrms doctypes; redu time-boxes `docker compose up -d` at 600s. That box expired mid-install, so the five containers gated on `service_completed_successfully` were left in state `created` and never started — the deployment went `error` at 1720s even though the site had been built perfectly (`create-site` exited 0). One `sudo docker compose up -d` on the VM started them in under a second, `create-site` re-ran into its "already exists, skipping" branch, and redu's own probe repaired the status to `ready`. Redeploying would have bought a second 15-minute site build and the identical timeout.

**Two corrections to the recipe, now written into `redu.md` as quirks:**
1. The verify script's check 2 greps for `Incorrect password`; this image says `Invalid login credentials`. It was reporting INCONCLUSIVE on a genuinely secure instance. I fixed `verify.sh` to match either wording *and* require `AuthenticationError` — the exception type is what separates a real refusal from a lockout.
2. **m1.mem16 is oversized.** Idle with all 11 containers: 1343 MB used of 15993 MB, ~620 MB of containers, disk 7.9 of 40.5 GB, zero OOM kills. m1.large (8 GB) is the better default at GBP 0.007/hr less. Caveat stated in the file: that's idle single-user data, not a payroll batch.

**Backups — done, not just described.** Took the first one (921 KB gzipped SQL) and pulled it **off the VM** to `backups/frappe-hr-first-backup.tar`. This matters more here than on your other deploys: there is no managed database, so `delete_deployment` takes the payroll data with it, and a backup sitting in the `sites` volume dies with the box. Put that one-line `ssh … tar -cf -` pipe on a schedule.

One thing to keep straight: the tag says `v16.16.0` but it's built from the **version-15** branches. You're running Frappe HR **v15**.

Files: `redu.md` (+4 quirks, deploy log, pinned dname — 24 quirks, YAML validated), `redu-deploy-plan.md` (real values replacing the estimate), `docker-compose.yml`, `verify.sh`, `.env`, `backups/`.
